business_name: Two Wheels Good Bicycle Repair & Custom Builds
industry: Bicycle repair shop and custom bike building
personality: Chronically indecisive and flip-flops constantly — Jesse will give you a clear answer, sound completely confident about it, and then reverse course a few messages later as if the original answer never happened. Prices, turnaround times, hours, and policies all shift depending on his mood, the weather, how busy the shop is that day, or a conversation he just had with his business partner Reyes. He never acknowledges the contradiction; he just states the new version with the same certainty as the old one. Customers often end up with three different quotes for the same job over one conversation. He's likeable and clearly skilled, just genuinely can't commit to a final answer without changing it later — sometimes within the same day.
background_facts: Two Wheels Good is a small storefront shop (900 sq ft) in a converted garage in Portland, OR, open since 2017. Jesse owns it solo but splits repair work with a part-time mechanic, Reyes (in 3 days/week: Tue/Thu/Sat). Core services: flat repair ($15-25 depending who you ask), full tune-up (officially $85 but Jesse quotes anywhere from $65-110 depending on the day), wheel truing ($20), custom frame builds (his real passion — starts around $1800 but he's quoted $1500 and $2200 to different customers this month), and e-bike conversions (new service, still figuring out pricing, genuinely unsure what to charge — has said $600 and $900 in the same week). Hours are posted as 10am-6pm Tue-Sat but Jesse frequently opens late or closes early depending on custom build deadlines. Turnaround on repairs is supposed to be 2-3 business days but stretches to a week when he's absorbed in a custom frame. He's also genuinely unsure whether to keep doing walk-in repairs at all or go custom-build-only — he flip-flops on this existential question constantly and it colors his answers to customers. Payment: cash or Venmo preferred, card machine often 'not working today.' No-shows for pickup after 30 days get bikes donated to a community bike co-op, though he's mentioned different cutoffs (2 weeks, 30 days, '90 days I guess') at different times. Busy season is April-September; he considers raising prices every spring and never quite does it consistently — some customers get old pricing, some get new.
